description: Team of 4 students from the University of Pennsylvania
summary:
Imagine being six hours into a spacewalk. You’re tired, your hands ache, and the air in your helmet is getting stale because the filter that cleans it is almost full. Your heart speeds up, you breathe faster, and your thinking gets a little slower. A typical alarm system beeps three separate times. A flight surgeon sees one problem. There’s too much CO2 in the air you’re breathing. It’s time to stop and rest.

Aegis brings that kind of thinking into the astronaut’s helmet. It watches their body, their suit, and their spacewalk plan, figures out what’s actually wrong, and gives one simple instruction. Non urgent reminders wait until the astronaut isn’t busy. Emergencies never wait. This same view shows the mission clock and which supply will run out first. Mission Control sees every reading.

We built this as a spacewalk you can try in your browser. It’s based on NASA’s model of the space station and NASA’s research on spaceflight risks. As we further space exploration, this will only become more important. On the Moon and Mars, an answer from Earth can take forty minutes. Aegis can answer in seconds.
details:
WHAT AEGIS DOES

Aegis is a health monitoring and triage system that lives inside the astronaut’s helmet display during a spacewalk (EVA). It watches the suit and the astronaut’s body, figures out what is actually going wrong, and shows one alert with one thing to do about it. Mission Control still gets every raw reading, each one labeled with the cause Aegis assigned it, so the flight surgeon can check our reasoning and make the final call.

We started from a simple observation. A spacewalk from the ISS lasts about six and a half hours of hard work in a suit filled with pure oxygen at 4.3 psi. The main health risks are CO₂ buildup, overheating, fatigue, hand strain and decompression sickness, and they tend to show up together. When the suit’s CO₂ scrubber starts filling up late in the walk, CO₂ rises in the helmet, and then breathing, heart rate and reaction time all get worse. A normal alarm system treats those as three or four separate problems. The astronaut is dealing with one.

HOW IT WORKS – KEY TECHNICAL INNOVATIONS

  1. Coupled suit and body model. We built a physiology model that updates every frame, and the readings affect each other the way they would in a real body. Harder work raises heart rate and CO₂ production. More CO₂ speeds up breathing and slows reactions. The temperature of the cooling garment (LCVG) changes core temperature. The model also tracks sleep debt, hydration, glucose, radiation dose and decompression sickness risk. The suit’s four consumables (oxygen, battery, cooling water and scrubber capacity) run down faster when the astronaut works harder.
    • a suit pressure warning
    • reported joint pain (possible decompression sickness)
    • 30 mL or more of water in the helmet
    • a CO₂ warning that lasts 300 mission seconds
  2. Knowing when not to interrupt. Aegis treats the astronaut as busy when they’re holding a handrail, moving along the station, or working above 72% of their maximum workload. While they’re busy, minor alerts wait. They show up after 1.5 seconds of calm, or after 10 minutes at most (20 for routine reminders). Urgent alerts and end-the-EVA calls always come through immediately. show alert = urgent or terminate, OR astronaut is calm, OR alert has waited its maximum time
  3. Avoiding alarm fatigue. A minor alert has to stay true for 20 seconds before it appears, and it stays up for 40 seconds after it clears, so a reading hovering on a threshold doesn’t make the display flicker. The top alert keeps its spot unless something more serious comes in. Suit tones play at most every 6 seconds (every second if something becomes urgent). Once the astronaut acknowledges an alert, it dims and only comes back if it gets worse.
  4. A display you control with your eyes. Alerts appear as small icons along the top of the visor, with the most serious first. Looking at one opens a card with the reading, what to do, and the numbers behind it. Pressing Start opens the matching check, and finishing the check acknowledges the alert. The corners of the visor fold away until you look at them. Eye tracking uses Google’s MediaPipe Face Landmarker, with a 9-point calibration, and runs entirely in the browser. You can use the mouse instead.
  5. Self-tests on a schedule. Aegis prompts the astronaut to test themselves before, during and after the walk. That includes the PVT-B reaction-time test every two hours, a mood and fatigue check-in using the Samn-Perelli scale every hour, a drink reminder every 40 minutes and a suit check every 45. For the PVT-B, we count any response of 355 ms or slower as a lapse. These results feed a wellbeing score that combines body readings (50%), reaction time (20%), how the astronaut says they feel (15%) and whether they kept up with the schedule (15%). The astronaut can also dictate notes for the ground, or look up a health question in onboard notes and NIH MedlinePlus.
  6. Predictions the flight surgeon can check by hand. Fatigue, heat, dehydration and CO₂ risk are simple weighted scores, and each one shows the reasons behind it. Together they produce a readiness call: go, go with adjustments, or review with the flight surgeon. If the predictions say the rest of the plan won’t work, Aegis suggests a change, like skipping an optional task. A person always has to accept it.
  7. A full record for Mission Control. Every frame streams to the Mission Control dashboard, and Supabase saves a snapshot about every 30 mission seconds. Each reading change shows up on its own line with its cause attached, for example O₂ CAUTION 22 % [cause:consumables]. When Aegis calls an end to the EVA, ground gets the numbers that triggered it. The dashboard also shows how long each reading stayed in range and, when the trend is clear enough, roughly when it will leave the safe range.

HOW A SPACEWALK CHANGES WITH AEGIS

Right now, health monitoring on a spacewalk is a team effort over the radio. Suit data goes down to Mission Control, where flight controllers and a flight surgeon watch it and talk the crew through problems. When several readings go off at once, the astronaut hears every alarm, usually while holding onto a handrail. Figuring out what’s actually wrong means waiting for that conversation with the ground.

Aegis moves that first step, figuring out the cause, into the helmet. The astronaut gets one alert and one action, at a moment when they can act on it, and serious problems still come through right away. Mission Control sees the same raw data it always has, plus Aegis’s cause labels. From the ground, they can change the self-test schedule, approve the plan or ask for a review, and send up a new plan for the astronaut to accept or decline.

CASE STUDY – A SPACEWALK THAT RUNS LONG

Here’s what happens in Aegis when an EVA starts running over time.

Ten minutes behind schedule, Aegis notes it in the background without interrupting. If the astronaut is also getting tired, the delay and the fatigue become a single alert telling them to skip the extra task and confirm the new plan with the crewmember guiding them from inside. Starting it opens a reaction-time test.

Because the walk is running long, oxygen and battery keep draining. A normal system would sound two alarms here. Aegis shows one “Consumables low” alert asking the astronaut to slow down and switch off helmet lights they don’t need. If they’re mid-climb on a handrail, the alert waits a moment. Once either reading hits the warning level, the alert becomes urgent, skips the wait, and tells them to head back to the airlock. Mission Control sees every reading the whole time, each labeled “fatigue” or “consumables,” so they can confirm the grouping was right.

You can also try scenario S9 in the scenario console, where helmet CO₂, heart rate and fatigue all rise together and Aegis traces them back to a single “Helmet CO₂ high” alert.

WHAT YOU CAN TRY

  • A first-person spacewalk around NASA’s ISS model. You can walk in low gravity and climb along more than 1,000 handrails pulled from the model, following lit rails to your worksite.
  • A visor display you control with your eyes. Windows open when you look at them, buttons select when you hold your gaze, and the visor fogs up when CO₂ or heat gets high.
  • Nine activities inside the visor, including the PVT-B, a fatigue check-in, paced breathing, a suit check on a 3D model of NASA’s spacesuit, a journal and a medical reference.
  • Ten scenarios from the scenario console (press G), including a slow suit leak, decompression sickness symptoms, and water in the helmet based on Luca Parmitano’s 2013 spacewalk.
  • The Mission Control dashboard (#/dashboard), with live charts and ECG, cause labels, the reasoning behind each prediction, trend analysis, and CSV/JSON import and export.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

We wrote Aegis in TypeScript with React 19 and Vite. The 3D scene uses three.js and react-three-fiber, with NASA’s ISS and spacesuit models from NASA 3D Resources and Blue Marble imagery from NASA Earth Observatory. App state lives in zustand. Eye tracking runs on MediaPipe Tasks Vision, suit sounds are synthesized with Web Audio, and dictation and read-aloud use the browser’s Web Speech API. Medical lookups come from NIH MedlinePlus. Sessions can be recorded to Supabase (Postgres), and the triage logic is covered by 169 automated tests in Vitest. The site is hosted on Vercel. All you need is a desktop browser that supports WebGL2, plus a webcam if you want eye tracking.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The main benefit is fewer, clearer alerts during the hardest part of a mission, without taking any information away from the ground. This matters more the farther crews go. A message to the Moon takes about 2.6 seconds round trip, and one to Mars can take up to about 44 minutes. That’s too long to wait for someone on Earth to explain an alarm. Aegis gives the astronaut a next step right away and leaves ground with the full record to review. Over many spacewalks, the self-test results would also build a baseline for each crewmember, so changes in reaction time or fatigue are easier to spot.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most monitoring tools add another screen of numbers. We spent most of our effort deciding when Aegis should stay quiet. It groups related readings into one alert, holds minor alerts until the astronaut’s hands are free, follows where they’re looking, and suggests plan changes without making them.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Attention. Astronauts’ hands and eyes are already busy, so every alert had to be short, ranked and well timed.
  • Who’s in charge. Serious problems escalate firmly, but the crew and the ground always have the last word on the plan.
  • Grounding in NASA research. Our features map to NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight and its EVA risk. The EVA timeline and consumables follow NASA’s “How to Plan a Spacewalk.” The self-tests are based on established instruments (PVT-B and Samn-Perelli). Eye closure (PERCLOS) is simulated for now.
  • Honesty. All crew data is made up, and our thresholds are illustrative, because the real spacesuit alarm limits aren’t public. Aegis isn’t a medical device, and the medical reference never diagnoses. Anything urgent goes to the ground.
  • Privacy. Eye tracking runs on the device and camera frames are never saved or sent. Voice input uses the browser’s speech recognition (in Chrome, Google processes the audio), and medical questions are sent to MedlinePlus.
  • Easy access for judges. Everything runs from one public link, with a presenter-mode deck as a backup.

We had a lot of fun creating this project. We hope this can help NASA astronauts balance their health and their tasks during spacewalks better!
